title: The Frontier, 1866–1869
summary: America a year after the Civil War, from Boston to San Francisco: the trails west, the railroads racing across the plains, the cattle drives, the gold camps, and the Native nations whose lands it all crosses. Make your own story anywhere, in a western town or a city of the coasts.
setting: The United States in the spring of 1866, a year after the Civil War. The East is rebuilding; the South is defeated and bitter, and four million freed people are claiming what freedom means. West of the Missouri lies the frontier: the Great Plains, the Rocky Mountains, the deserts and the Pacific coast, crossed by wagon trails, stage lines and the telegraph. The Union Pacific is laying track west from Omaha and the Central Pacific east from Sacramento, racing to meet. Miners chase gold and silver, Texans look for a railroad to sell their longhorns to, and settlers claim homesteads, all of it on the lands of the Plains and mountain nations, who fight, treat and hold on as their situations demand.
toneNote: A big, hard country: weeks of travel, weather and work, broken by sudden danger. Violence is quick and has weight. Native nations are peoples with their own leaders and reasons, never a backdrop; the racism of the time is shown honestly, never celebrated.
rules: History runs on: railroads, treaties, wars and elections happen on their dates; the story is what ordinary people do inside them.
News travels by telegraph along the lines, else by stage and word of mouth, days or weeks late.
Travel is slow: a wagon makes fifteen miles a good day, rivers run high in spring, passes close with the snow.
Law is thin in the West: an army post, a sheriff, a vigilance committee, or nothing.
Guns are everywhere and violence is sudden; a wound far from a doctor can kill.
The Native nations have their own leaders, alliances and reasons: they trade, hunt, negotiate, raid and fight as their situations demand.

roles.label: Homesteader
roles.desc: Filed on a quarter section and means to prove it up: sod, plough, well and weather.

roles.label: Drover
roles.desc: Rides herd on longhorns: long days in the saddle, river crossings and stampedes.

roles.label: Prospector
roles.desc: Follows every rumour of colour in a creek, with a pan, a pick and a mule.

roles.label: Freighter
roles.desc: Drives a team of oxen or mules hauling goods across the plains for the freight lines.

roles.label: Railroad worker
roles.desc: Grades, lays track or swings a spike maul for the railroad, and drinks in the end-of-track tents.

roles.label: Veteran
roles.desc: Fought in the war, blue or grey, and came west to forget it or to start again.

roles.label: Scout
roles.desc: Knows the country, its peoples and their languages; guides the army, a wagon train or a survey party.

roles.label: Storekeeper
roles.desc: Runs a store, a saloon or a boarding house, and knows everyone's debts.

roles.label: Doctor
roles.desc: Trained back East or in an army hospital; sets bones, pulls bullets and fights cholera.

roles.label: Gambler
roles.desc: Lives on cards, nerve and reading people, from one boomtown to the next.

roles.label: Teacher or preacher
roles.desc: Came west to teach school or keep a church in a town that has neither yet.

roles.label: Hunter of a Plains nation
roles.desc: A hunter and rider of one of the Plains nations, at home on the land the others only cross.

locations.name: Front Street
locations.desc: A wide dirt street facing the railroad grade, with a row of plank-and-canvas businesses along its north side and town-lot stakes everywhere.

locations.name: The Railhead saloon
locations.desc: A tent saloon on a plank floor: a bar of boards on barrels, a faro table, and graders spending their pay.

locations.name: Kittredge's mercantile
locations.desc: A canvas-roofed store stacked with flour sacks, coffee, tinned goods, boots, rope and cartridges, at railroad prices.

locations.name: The engineers' office
locations.desc: A board shack where the railroad's engineers keep their maps, instruments and the plat of the town to be.

locations.name: The boarding house
locations.desc: Two storeys of green lumber where the railroad's men sleep four to a room and eat in shifts at a long table.

locations.name: Blacksmith and wagon shop
locations.desc: An open-fronted shop that rings from dawn: grading scrapers, wagon tyres and mule shoes.

locations.name: Freight corral and mule pens
locations.desc: Pole corrals full of the grading contractors' mules, and freight wagons waiting to be unloaded.

locations.name: The back lots and soddies
locations.desc: Behind the business row: sod houses, dugouts, privies, a dug well and staked lots where the town will grow.

locations.name: Depot ground and section house
locations.desc: The railroad's ground between the street and the grade: the section house half built, the frame of a water tank, stacks of ties.

locations.name: Tent row
locations.desc: The graders' camp: rows of canvas tents, cook fires and washing lines, louder every night.

locations.name: The road ranch
locations.desc: An older sod road ranch on the river road, where the stages change horses and emigrants buy feed and whiskey.

locations.name: The grade
locations.desc: The raised bed of the railroad, graded and waiting for ties and rails, running dead straight east and west out of sight.

locations.name: The Platte bottoms
locations.desc: The river's wide sandy bottoms: braided channels, cottonwoods, and the emigrant road on the far bank.

locations.name: Front Street
locations.desc: The town's one real street, rutted by cattle and wagons, false fronts on both sides and a plank sidewalk on the north.

locations.name: The Drovers' Rest
locations.desc: The biggest saloon in town: a long bar, mirrors freighted from St. Louis, card tables, and Texans who haven't been paid yet.

locations.name: The Cattleman's Hotel
locations.desc: Two storeys with a porch, the only beds with sheets for fifty miles; cattle buyers and speculators talk business in its dining room.

locations.name: Land and stock office
locations.desc: A narrow office where the town company sells lots and a stock buyer offers Texans a fraction of what their cattle would bring at a railhead.

locations.name: General store
locations.desc: Everything from saddles to calico to coffee, sold on credit to people the storekeeper trusts.

locations.name: Livery stable and corral
locations.desc: A big barn and a corral at the east end, horses for hire and sale, and a loft where drifters sleep for a dime.

locations.name: Back alley
locations.desc: A muddy lane behind the north side: privies, woodpiles, back doors and the town's quieter business.

locations.name: Marshal's office and jail
locations.desc: A stone-walled office with two iron cells, a rack of rifles and a list of town ordinances nobody reads.

locations.name: Blacksmith
locations.desc: A smithy shoeing the drovers' horses and mending branding irons.

locations.name: The dance hall
locations.desc: A barn of a building with a fiddler, a piano with half its keys, and dances sold by the ticket.

locations.name: Schoolhouse and chapel
locations.desc: One whitewashed room: school on weekdays, preaching on Sundays, town meetings when there's trouble.

locations.name: Stage station
locations.desc: The Smoky Hill stage stop: a sod-and-plank office, a corral of fresh horses and the mail.

locations.name: The shipping pens
locations.desc: Big plank pens and loading chutes at the west end, built by a speculator for a railroad that hasn't come yet.

locations.name: The herd grounds
locations.desc: Open prairie east of town where the Texas herds graze and wait, watched by night riders.

locations.name: The Saline ford
locations.desc: The shallow crossing below town, cottonwoods along the bank and the stage road climbing out the far side.

locations.name: The Overland road
locations.desc: The stage and emigrant road along the South Platte, deep in dust, the station buildings on its north side.

locations.name: The stage station
locations.desc: The Overland's home station, rebuilt in sod after the burning of last year: a low long room with a table for passengers.

locations.name: Telegraph office
locations.desc: A sod office with a key and a sounder: the only fast news for two hundred miles, and the line goes down often.

locations.name: Store and saloon
locations.desc: A warehouse store that sells whiskey at one end and everything else at the other, at prices that make emigrants swear.

locations.name: Stage stable and corrals
locations.desc: A long sod stable and corrals for the stage teams, with a guard on the horses at night.

locations.name: Blacksmith
locations.desc: A smith who keeps the coaches running: wheels, springs, shoes.

locations.name: Fort Sedgwick
locations.desc: The army post up the road: sod barracks, a flagstaff and a parade ground of bare dirt, and cavalry who are rarely all present.

locations.name: Sutler's store
locations.desc: The post sutler's store, where soldiers buy tobacco on credit and officers drink.

locations.name: Emigrant campground
locations.desc: Trampled ground between road and river where wagon companies circle for the night.

locations.name: The South Platte crossing
locations.desc: A mile of shallow, quicksand-bottomed river, crossed by wagons with doubled teams.

locations.name: Across the river
locations.desc: Empty bottomland across the river where railroad surveyors' stakes run in a line toward the west.

locations.name: The trail down from the pass
locations.desc: A faint wagon track off the South Pass road, down through sage and rock into the gulch.

locations.name: Tent row
locations.desc: A dozen patched tents and brush shelters along the creek, washing hung on the willows.

locations.name: The cook fire
locations.desc: A stone fire ring under a canvas fly, the camp's one kettle and its very small store of flour and bacon.

locations.name: The cabin
locations.desc: The only log cabin, half roofed, where the camp keeps its gold dust and its arguments.

locations.name: The creek and the diggings
locations.desc: The creek, dammed and ditched, with rockers and a sluice; gravel heaps along both banks.

locations.name: The discovery claim
locations.desc: Upstream, the claim where the first colour was panned, marked with a notice on a post.

locations.name: The staked town
locations.desc: A flat above the creek laid out with stakes and string: a main street, lots and a square, for a town that doesn't exist yet.

locations.name: Lookout ridge
locations.desc: A rocky rise with a view east along the trail toward the pass, where someone always watches for wagons.

locations.name: The camp circle
locations.desc: The lodges of Tall Grass's band pitched in a wide circle opening to the east, smoke rising from their tops, dogs and children everywhere.

locations.name: The council lodge
locations.desc: The big lodge at the head of the circle where the men who lead talk, smoke and decide.

locations.name: A family lodge
locations.desc: A lodge of painted buffalo hides: robes, parfleches, a fire in the middle, a family's whole life.

locations.name: The work ground
locations.desc: Behind the lodges where hides are staked and scraped, meat dried and the women of the camp work and talk.

locations.name: The horse herd
locations.desc: The camp's horses grazing on the bottomland, the wealth of every family, watched by the boys day and night.

locations.name: The lookout hill
locations.desc: A rise above the camp where the young men watch the country for buffalo, enemies and strangers.

locations.name: The river
locations.desc: Cottonwoods and willow along the water, where the camp drinks, bathes and fetches wood.

standees.label: Irish graders
standees.note: Paid on Saturdays; drunk by Saturday night.

standees.label: Texas drovers

timeline.text: President Lincoln signed the Homestead Act: 160 acres of public land to anyone who lives on it and works it for five years.
Congress chartered the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific to build a railroad and telegraph to the Pacific, with land and loans for every mile.
After the Dakota War in Minnesota, thirty-eight Dakota men were hanged together at Mankato, and their people were driven from the state.
The Central Pacific broke ground at Sacramento, building east toward the Sierra Nevada.
The Union Pacific broke ground at Omaha, building west across Nebraska.
After the army burned their fields and orchards, thousands of Diné were marched three hundred miles to Bosque Redondo by Fort Sumner; many died on the way.
Colorado volunteers attacked Black Kettle's Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek, which flew an American flag, and killed about two hundred people, most of them women, children and the old.
In revenge for Sand Creek, Cheyenne, Lakota and Arapaho warriors raided Julesburg twice and burned the station and the town.
General Lee surrendered the Army of Northern Virginia to General Grant at Appomattox Court House; the Civil War was over.
President Lincoln was shot at Ford's Theatre and died the next morning; Andrew Johnson became president.
General Connor's columns marched into the Powder River country, attacked an Arapaho village on the Tongue River, and came back half starved.
The Thirteenth Amendment was ratified: slavery is abolished everywhere in the United States.
Congress passed the Civil Rights Act over President Johnson's veto: everyone born here is a citizen, with equal rights in law.
For three days white mobs, police among them, attacked the Black neighbourhoods of Memphis, killing dozens and burning homes, churches and schools.
Two Texas cattlemen set out west with two thousand longhorns along the Pecos, to sell beef to the army at Fort Sumner.
At the treaty council at Fort Laramie, Red Cloud walked out when soldiers marched in to build forts on the Bozeman Trail before anything was agreed; he vowed to close the road.

groups.stance: at war over the Bozeman Trail

timeline.text: The spring rise is over: the rivers are falling and the fords are open again.
Colonel Carrington's soldiers began building a stockade fort on Piney Creek, in the heart of the Powder River country: Fort Phil Kearny.
The Cherokee Nation signed a new treaty in Washington: freedom and citizenship for the people it had held enslaved, and land in the west given up for other nations and for railroads.
Congress reorganized the army, with four regiments of Black soldiers among the new ones: two of cavalry, two of infantry.
In New Orleans, police and a white mob attacked a convention for Black voting rights and killed dozens of Black men.
The Union Pacific's track reached the Fort Kearny station; trains now run from Omaha to the end of track.
The Union Pacific's track reached Haddon at the hundredth meridian, and a special train brought senators, newspapermen and a brass band out to celebrate.
The Radical Republicans swept the congressional elections; Congress will now take Reconstruction out of President Johnson's hands.
Snow has closed the mountain passes and the Sierra for the winter.
The upper Missouri has fallen too low for the steamboats; the last ones have gone downriver until spring.
The Central Pacific's track reached Cisco, high in the Sierra; Chinese crews are cutting tunnels through the granite at the summit.
The Union Pacific's track reached the forks of the Platte, its end of track for the winter, and the gamblers and saloons moved on with it.
Eighty-one soldiers under Captain Fetterman were drawn out of Fort Phil Kearny and killed to the last man by Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors.
The Chicago and North Western reached Council Bluffs, across the river from Omaha: by rail from the East to the Missouri at last.
Nebraska was admitted to the Union as the thirty-seventh state.
Congress passed the Reconstruction Acts over the President's veto: the South is put under the army in five military districts until its states give Black men the vote.
Secretary Seward signed a treaty buying Russian America, Alaska, for seven million dollars; the papers call it his folly.
General Hancock's soldiers burned an abandoned Cheyenne and Lakota village on Pawnee Fork; war spread along the Smoky Hill all summer.
The spring rise has the rivers running high and fast; the fords are dangerous again.
The snow is off the passes; the mountain roads and the Sierra are open again.
The railroad's track reached Salt Lick: the shipping pens have a railroad at last, and word is riding south to the Texas herds.
The Union Pacific's track reached Julesburg; within weeks a town of tents, saloons and gambling halls has sprung up across the river, four thousand strong.
The spring rise is over: the rivers are falling and the fords are open again.
The Union Pacific's surveyors laid out a town where the line will cross Crow Creek and named it Cheyenne; lots sold within days.
Near Fort Phil Kearny, soldiers with new breech-loading rifles held off a large Lakota attack from behind a corral of wagon boxes.
Cheyenne warriors pulled up the rails near Plum Creek and wrecked a Union Pacific freight train in the night.
The first Texas herd of the year was loaded into cattle cars at Salt Lick, bound for Chicago; the drovers have been paid and are spending it.
The upper Missouri has fallen too low for the steamboats until spring.
At Medicine Lodge Creek, Comanche, Kiowa, Southern Cheyenne, Arapaho and Plains Apache leaders signed treaties for reservations in Indian Territory, with hunting rights below the Arkansas.
The Union Pacific's track reached Cheyenne, and the end-of-track town moved there from Julesburg on flatcars.
Snow has closed the mountain passes and the Sierra for the winter.
The city of Roxbury became part of Boston.
The House of Representatives impeached President Johnson; the Senate will try him.
Lakota leaders began signing a treaty at Fort Laramie: a great reservation with the Black Hills, the Powder River country left to them, and the Bozeman forts to be abandoned.

groups.stance: Red Cloud waits for the forts to be gone

timeline.text: The spring rise has the rivers running high and fast; the fords are dangerous again.
The Senate failed by a single vote to remove President Johnson from office.
The snow is off the passes; the mountain roads and the Sierra are open again.
At Bosque Redondo the Diné signed a treaty that lets them go home: a reservation in their own country, and the long walk back begins.
The Central Pacific's first train came over the Sierra and down to the Truckee Meadows: rails from Sacramento to Nevada.
The spring rise is over: the rivers are falling and the fords are open again.
At Fort Bridger, Washakie's Eastern Shoshone signed a treaty for a reservation in the Wind River valley.
The Fourteenth Amendment was ratified: citizenship for everyone born here, and the equal protection of the laws.
Congress made the western part of Dakota Territory, from the Black Hills to the Wasatch, into Wyoming Territory.

region_status.status: cut in two: the west is Wyoming Territory since July 1868

timeline.text: The soldiers marched out of the Bozeman Trail forts, and Red Cloud's warriors burned Fort Phil Kearny behind them.
On the Arikaree, Cheyenne and Lakota warriors besieged fifty army scouts on an island for nine days; the warrior Roman Nose was killed.
General Grant was elected president.
Red Cloud came in to Fort Laramie and signed the treaty, now that the forts were gone.

groups.stance: at peace by treaty, the Powder River country theirs

timeline.text: Snow has closed the mountain passes for the winter; the Central Pacific keeps its trains running through the Sierra under snow sheds.
At dawn Custer's Seventh Cavalry attacked Black Kettle's Cheyenne camp on the Washita; Black Kettle and his wife were killed with dozens of their people.
Ulysses S. Grant was sworn in as president.
The spring rise has the rivers running high and fast; the fords are dangerous again.
The Union Pacific and the Central Pacific met at Promontory Summit in Utah; a golden spike was driven, and the telegraph flashed one word across the country: "Done."
The snow is off the passes; the mountain roads are open again.
A one-armed veteran, Major Powell, set out down the Green River with nine men and four boats to explore the canyons of the Colorado.
At Summit Springs soldiers and Pawnee scouts attacked Tall Bull's Dog Soldier camp; Tall Bull was killed, and the Dog Soldiers' war was broken.
Wyoming Territory gave women the vote, the first place in the country to do so.
The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified: no citizen may be denied the vote because of race.

regions.name: The United States
regions.label: country
regions.status: a year after the Civil War; the South under Reconstruction
regions.lore: Thirty-six states and the western territories under President Andrew Johnson. The Union won the war; what the peace means is the great quarrel.

regions.name: The Northeast
regions.label: section
regions.lore: Factories, railroads, banks and immigrant cities: the money behind the railroads west.

regions.name: The Midwest
regions.label: section
regions.lore: Farm states between the Ohio and the Missouri; Chicago and St. Louis are the gateways west.

regions.name: The South
regions.label: section
regions.lore: The defeated Confederacy: burned towns, freed people claiming land and schools, old planters passing Black Codes.

regions.name: The Great Plains
regions.label: section
regions.lore: Buffalo grasslands from the Missouri to the Rockies, crossed by the trails and the new railroads.

regions.name: The Mountain West
regions.label: section
regions.lore: The Rockies, the Great Basin and the southwestern deserts: mining camps, Mormon towns and army posts.

regions.name: The Pacific Coast
regions.label: section
regions.lore: California, Oregon and Washington, rich from gold and timber, a month from the East by sea.

regions.name: British North America
regions.label: country
regions.lore: The British colonies to the north, uneasy about American designs on them; the Hudson's Bay Company still holds the prairies to the west.

regions.name: Mexico
regions.label: country
regions.lore: A French-backed emperor, Maximilian, fights a war against President Juárez's republicans; the United States wants the French gone.

regions.name: Texas
regions.label: state
regions.lore: A defeated Confederate state with millions of longhorn cattle running loose on its ranges and no market to sell them in; Comanche and Kiowa raids along its western edge.

regions.name: Kansas
regions.label: state
regions.lore: A free state scarred by the border war; settlers push west along the Smoky Hill.

regions.name: Nebraska Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.status: a territory, soon to be a state
regions.lore: Settled along the Missouri; the Platte valley carries the emigrant roads, the stage, the telegraph and now the railroad.

regions.name: Dakota Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: A vast territory, almost all of it Lakota country; Fort Laramie and the emigrant roads cross its southwest.

regions.name: Indian Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: Land set aside for nations removed from the East: the Cherokee, Creek, Choctaw, Chickasaw and Seminole govern themselves here, divided and ruined by the war, in which many of them sided with the Confederacy.

regions.name: The Neutral Strip
regions.label: unorganized land
regions.lore: A strip of grass belonging to no state or territory, used by Comanche and Kiowa hunters and by people who want no law at all.

regions.name: Montana Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: A new territory of gold camps in the mountains, reached by the Missouri steamboats to Fort Benton, the road from Salt Lake, or the Bozeman Trail.

regions.name: Idaho Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: Gold camps in the Boise Basin and the Clearwater, the Oregon Trail along the Snake, and the lands of the Nez Perce, Shoshone and Bannock.

regions.name: Colorado Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: A mining territory along the Front Range, centred on Denver; still bitter and divided over Sand Creek.

regions.name: Utah Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: The Latter-day Saints' territory, irrigated and orderly, governed in practice from Brigham Young's office in Great Salt Lake City.

regions.name: Nevada
regions.label: state
regions.lore: A new state built on the silver of the Comstock Lode, its desert crossed by the California Trail and the Overland stage.

regions.name: New Mexico Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: Old Hispanic towns and villages along the Rio Grande, Pueblo peoples, army forts, and the end of the Santa Fe Trail.

regions.name: Arizona Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: A desert territory of a few towns and mines, at war with the Apache since the soldiers left for the Civil War and came back.

regions.name: California
regions.label: state
regions.lore: Rich, proud and far away: San Francisco's banks, the gold country of the Sierra foothills, wheat in the Central Valley, and a large Chinese community that does much of the hardest work.

regions.name: Oregon
regions.label: state
regions.lore: The end of the Oregon Trail: farms in the Willamette Valley, Portland on the river, and Oregon City where the emigrants file their claims.

regions.name: Washington Territory
regions.label: territory
regions.lore: Forests, sawmills and Puget Sound, still thinly settled, with Walla Walla in the dry country east of the mountains.

regions.name: Powder River Country
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: Rich hunting country east of the Bighorn Mountains, won by the Lakota and their allies from the Crow. The Bozeman Trail to the Montana gold camps cuts straight through it.

regions.name: The Black Hills (Paha Sapa)
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: Paha Sapa, pine-dark hills rising from the plains, sacred to the Lakota and a place they go for timber, game and prayer.

regions.name: The Wind River country
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: Mountain valleys north of South Pass, the homeland the Eastern Shoshone under Washakie want to keep for their own.

regions.name: The Smoky Hill and Republican country
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The buffalo range along the Smoky Hill and Republican rivers, the hunting grounds of the Southern Cheyenne and the Dog Soldiers; the stage line along it has been attacked again and again.

regions.name: Comanchería (the Llano Estacado)
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The Llano Estacado and the high plains: Comanche and Kiowa country, crossed by no road anyone else trusts.

regions.name: The Ute country
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The high valleys and parks west of the Front Range, the Ute peoples' home; miners push in every summer.

regions.name: Apachería (the Apache country)
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: Mountains and desert between the Gila and the Mexican line, where Apache bands keep their own country against miners, ranchers and soldiers.

regions.name: Dinétah (the Navajo country)
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The Diné homeland between the four sacred mountains: canyons, mesas and burned peach orchards, nearly empty since the people were marched away; a few hold out in the canyons.

regions.name: The Crow country (the Yellowstone)
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The valley of the Yellowstone and the Bighorns, the Crow's country, pressed hard by the Lakota from the east.

regions.name: The Blackfeet country
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The plains below the British line and the mountains of the Continental Divide, the Blackfoot Confederacy's land; whiskey traders and miners are trouble.

regions.name: The Nez Perce country (the Clearwater)
regions.label: homeland
regions.lore: The Clearwater and Snake river country of the Nez Perce, shrunk by the treaty of 1863 after gold was found; the bands who never signed it still live in the Wallowa.

regions.name: Boston
regions.label: city
regions.lore: An old, proud, crowded port: Yankee merchants and mill money on Beacon Hill, Irish families in the North End and Fort Hill, abolitionist pulpits and newspapers. The city is filling in the Back Bay to build itself new land.

regions.name: Denver
regions.label: town
regions.lore: The supply town of Colorado's gold country, all brick and frame after the great fire, at the end of the stage lines.

regions.name: Great Salt Lake City
regions.label: city
regions.lore: The Saints' city, laid out in wide square blocks with water running in ditches down every street; the Tabernacle is going up beside the unfinished temple.

regions.name: San Francisco
regions.label: city
regions.lore: The West's great city, built on gold and now on Comstock silver: banks and mansions on the hills, the Barbary Coast's saloons by the docks, Chinatown, and ships from every ocean. It got its law from vigilance committees and hasn't forgotten.

regions.name: Virginia City (the Comstock)
regions.label: town
regions.lore: Built on the Comstock Lode: deep silver mines, mansions, opera, saloons, and a newspaper where a young humorist has been making his name.

regions.name: Virginia City (Alder Gulch)
regions.label: town
regions.lore: Montana's richest gold camp on Alder Gulch, where vigilantes hanged the road agents two winters ago.

regions.name: Omaha
regions.label: town
regions.lore: A raw river town on the Missouri, headquarters of the Union Pacific.

regions.name: Haddon
regions.label: town
regions.status: staked out, waiting for the rails
regions.lore: A station town platted by the railroad on the Platte at the hundredth meridian: a street of plank and canvas, waiting for the track.

regions.name: Salt Lick
regions.label: town
regions.status: a cattle town without a railroad yet
regions.lore: A Kansas town on the Saline, built on credit for a railroad not yet here; Texas herds wait on the prairie east of it.

regions.name: Julesburg
regions.label: town
regions.lore: A sod stage station and store on the South Platte where the Denver road leaves the Overland trail, burned last year and rebuilt, with Fort Sedgwick up the road.

regions.name: Poorman's Gulch
regions.label: camp
regions.lore: A gulch north of South Pass where a few poor prospectors found gold and told no one.

regions.name: Fort Kearny
regions.label: fort
regions.lore: An army post on the Platte where the trails from the Missouri meet.

regions.name: The Pawnee reservation (the Loup)
regions.label: reservation
regions.lore: Pawnee earth-lodge villages on the Loup, raided by the Lakota and Cheyenne.

regions.name: Fort Laramie
regions.label: fort
regions.lore: The great post on the Oregon Trail at the North Platte, once a fur-trade fort: emigrants rest, trade and write letters here, and treaty councils meet.

regions.name: South Pass
regions.label: landmark
regions.lore: The broad, gentle saddle across the Continental Divide that made the Oregon Trail possible; the waters run west from here.

regions.name: Fort Phil Kearny
regions.label: fort
regions.lore: A stockade fort on Piney Creek guarding the Bozeman Trail.

regions.name: Cheyenne (Crow Creek Crossing)
regions.label: town
regions.lore: A railroad town on Crow Creek.

regions.name: Dutch Flat and the Sierra grade
regions.label: camp
regions.lore: A gold town in the Sierra foothills, now the Central Pacific's base: Chinese grading camps, blasting powder and the wagon road over Donner Summit.

regions.name: Bosque Redondo (Fort Sumner)
regions.label: reservation
regions.lore: A reservation by Fort Sumner on the Pecos where the army holds the Diné and some Mescalero Apache: bad water, failed crops, alkali and disease.

regions.name: The Red River crossing
regions.label: landmark
regions.lore: Where the cattle trails from Texas cross the Red River into Indian Territory: quicksand, flood and the Chickasaw toll takers.
